fields.title: Business logic: what objects make up the product
fields.keyTakeaway: Before screens, you need to name system objects, their states, and state transition rules. Half of late reworks stem from an overlooked object or an unagreed state.
fields.checkQuestion: In Dispetcher, a trip was canceled after departure. What state is this, and how does it differ from "canceled" before departure?
fields.blocks/0/text: The key question of this node: **what objects make up the product system?** This is the most underrated node in the domain: people skip it and go straight to layouts.
fields.blocks/1/text: **What happens if you do not answer this question.** Development begins, and two weeks later it turns out that "driver" and "employee" are different entities with different permissions, that a trip has five states instead of two, and that the system fundamentally cannot represent cancellation after departure. Rework costs more than the feature itself.
fields.blocks/2/items/0: **What is it**—a domain noun: trip, order, driver, car, waybill.
fields.blocks/2/items/1: **Which attributes**—only those someone looks at or filters by.
fields.blocks/2/items/2: **Which connections and how many**—one trip to how many drivers? One driver to how many cars? Errors happen most often here.
fields.blocks/2/items/3: **Which states and transitions**—which state moves to which, who has permission, and what happens to other objects as a result.
fields.blocks/3/text:
States: draft → scheduled → assigned to driver → en route → completed.
Plus two the team initially missed:
"canceled before departure"—car and driver are freed, order returns to pool;
"interrupted"—car on the road, cargo partially delivered, a new trip is needed for the remainder.

The difference is not cosmetic: in the second case, a new object appears—cargo remainder—and there is nowhere to put it.

An hour spent on the state table at the start saved rewriting the planner.
fields.blocks/4/text: "A trip has one driver" is true until long-haul routes with driver swaps come along. Ask a dispatcher if that happened last month: usually, it did.
fields.blocks/4/title: Test "one-to-many" relationships with a real example
fields.blocks/5/text: **How this looks in practice.** A simple table is enough: object, states, who changes it, what happens to neighboring objects. It is more useful to a developer than a mockup and shows you gaps before paying for them.
fields.blocks/6/text: An entity model is not a database schema. Your task is to agree on the domain meaning and rules; how it is stored is up to engineering.
